problem: The claim that '8085 conditional jumps use an 8-bit offset relative to the program counter' is false. The 8085 has no program-counter-relative branching at all: JMP and every conditional jump (JZ, JC, JNC, etc.) carry a full 16-bit absolute address in the instruction. The 8-bit signed PC offset belongs to the 8051 (SJMP, JZ rel, DJNZ rel), so a student could carry the wrong fact into the exam and also mis-answer a question on why 8085 code is not position independent.
fix: Relative mode adds a signed offset to the program counter. 8086 JMP SHORT label adds an 8-bit displacement to IP, and 8051 SJMP label adds an 8-bit offset relative to the program counter. The 8085 has no relative branch: its JMP and conditional jumps hold a 16-bit absolute address, so 8085 code cannot simply be moved in memory.

problem: '8086 PUSH AX stores AX at [SP] and then subtracts 2 from SP' gives the wrong order and the wrong final location. On the 8086, SP is decremented first and AX is then written at the new SP. As written, a student would conclude the pushed word sits at the old top-of-stack address, which is exactly one word too high. It also contradicts the 8085 sentence just before it.
fix: 8086 PUSH AX subtracts 2 from SP first and then stores AX at the new [SP], so the word ends up at the address SP-2. POP AX does the reverse: read the word at [SP], then add 2 to SP.

problem: The sentence says RISC-V and ARM 'add scaled index modes for arrays of 2, 4 or 8 bytes'. ARM does have scaled register offsets (a shift applied to the index register), but base RISC-V has no scaled index mode: the index must be converted to a byte offset with a shift instruction before the load or store. Only x86-64 scales the index inside the instruction, through the SIB scale factor.
fix: ARM (A32) allows a shift on the index register inside the load/store, and x86-64 scales the index by 1, 2, 4 or 8 with the SIB byte. RISC-V keeps it simple: a load or store uses base plus immediate offset only, so the compiler must compute the byte offset of an array element with a separate shift or multiply.
